content: The public domain refers to a collection of knowledge and creative works, such as literature, art, music, and inventions, that are not subject to proprietary rights like copyright or patents. These works are considered part of a shared cultural and intellectual heritage, freely available for use by anyone for both commercial and non-commercial purposes. Approximately 15% of all books, including 10% of those still in print, are in the public domain. If a work is not in the public domain, it is typically protected by legal rights such as copyright or patents, which limit public use until those rights expire. Once these protections lapse, the work enters the public domain and can be used by anyone without restriction. A creative work is considered to be in the public domain if no laws restrict its use by the public. This can occur if no proprietary rights are established over the work or if the work is explicitly excluded from legal protections. However, because intellectual property laws vary by jurisdiction, a work may be in the public domain in one country but not in another. For example, some literary works are public domain in the United States but remain protected in the European Union, and vice versa. While the underlying ideas expressed in a work cannot be copyrighted, their specific expression can be. For instance, mathematical formulas are generally public domain, but their implementation in software may be protected by copyright or patents. Works created before the establishment of copyright and patent laws, such as the Bible or the inventions of Archimedes, are also part of the public domain. However, translations or new adaptations of these works may still be copyrighted. While facts themselves cannot be copyrighted, creative compilations or presentations of facts, such as categorized lists, may be protected. In some countries, database rights provide copyright-like protections even for collections of mere facts. For example, the European Union has a sui generis database rights regime. Government works in many countries, including those of the United States, are excluded from copyright and are therefore in the public domain. However, works created by contractors for the government may still be subject to copyright. Even public domain documents may have restricted availability if they contain classified information. Copyrights and patents have always had finite terms, after which the works or inventions enter the public domain. For most countries, patents expire after 20 years. Copyright terms are more complex and vary by jurisdiction. In general, a published work’s copyright expires when one of the following conditions is met: the work was created and first published before January 1, 1923, or at least 95 years before the current year; the last surviving author died at least 70 years ago; or no perpetual copyright laws have been enacted in the relevant jurisdiction. For example, in the United States, works created by federal agencies are public domain upon creation, but works created by contractors are not. In the United States, copyright law has undergone significant changes. Before 1978, unpublished works were protected under common law copyright, which was perpetual. The Copyright Act of 1976 abolished common law copyright, bringing all works under federal statutory copyright. For works created before 1978 but not published until after December 31, 2002, federal copyright protection lasts until 2047. Sound recordings fixed before February 15, 1972, were not covered by federal copyright law but were protected under state laws or common law until February 15, 2067. Critics of copyright term extensions argue that Congress has effectively created perpetual copyright through incremental extensions. For example, British government works are protected under Crown Copyright, which lasts 50 years from publication unless the author assigned the copyright to the Crown. Unpublished Crown Copyright documents become public domain 125 years after creation. However, no unpublished works will enter the public domain under this provision until 2039 due to legislative changes in 1989. In Canada and New Zealand, copyright terms remain the life of the author plus 50 years, as they have not adopted the 20-year extensions seen in the United States and Europe. Australia extended its copyright term by 20 years in 2004 but did not revive expired copyrights. Consequently, works by authors who died before 1955 remain in the public domain in Australia. Similarly, New Zealand has a longer Crown Copyright term of 100 years from publication. In Thailand, copyright lasts for the life of the author plus 50 years. For works by legal entities or anonymous authors, the term is 50 years from publication. Thai state documents are in the public domain. In Japan, copyright law does not explicitly mention the public domain, leading to potential use restrictions even for works considered public domain. Pre-1953 films, both Japanese and non-Japanese, are generally public domain in Japan. Examples of public domain works include the inventions of Thomas Edison, the writings of Carlo Collodi, and most works by Mozart and Mark Twain. However, some works, such as J.M. Barrie’s Peter Pan, have special legal protections that require royalties for performances in the UK, as the rights were bequeathed to Great Ormond Street Hospital in perpetuity. In the past, works in the United States could enter the public domain if released without a copyright notice. This changed after March 1, 1989, when copyright automatically attached to works fixed in a tangible medium. While it is commonly believed that it is impossible to place a work in the public domain, this is not entirely accurate. Authors can dedicate their works to the public domain, though the legal mechanisms for doing so are somewhat unclear. Judicial rulings, such as Computer Associates Int’l v. Altai, have established that computer software can enter the public domain through widespread dissemination or by becoming commonplace in the industry. In summary, the public domain encompasses a wide range of works and inventions that are free from proprietary restrictions, allowing for their unrestricted use and dissemination. However, the legal framework governing the public domain varies significantly across jurisdictions, and the process of dedicating works to the public domain remains a complex and evolving area of law.
